doc.title: Fred Wesley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 21, 2024

title: Bebop versus one-chord improvising; bassists Buster Williams and Ron Carter
summary: Playing up and down on one chord versus following bebop changes, then Buster Williams and Ron Carter playing funk lines on upright bass.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: We’ll think of it later, you know, after we sign off we’ll probably both think of it.
Yeah.
Well you were enamored early on with bebop.
Yeah.

Is there a difference and a challenge either way about improvising on a bebop tune with multiple chord changes and often times at a fast tempo rather than improvising on one chord. What’s the difference that’s going on in your head between those two?

Well on one chord you have to vary what you play, you have to make it sound like it’s a lot of chords you know. I guess you would play different things the same way you know. I can’t explain it exactly but with one chord you would do, you could up and down, the music goes up and down rather than sideways. You know? But for bebop you’ve got total freedom to follow the changes, right? But when you only have one change then you have to play it up and down. Do you understand? Up and down is better than sideways. It’s a different approach to the way you do it. You know?
I remember referring to — reading about Coleman Hawkins that way, that they were talking about he played vertical instead of horizontal.
Right. Vertical, horizontal.
Something like that. And certainly you’ve got a rhythmic aspect when you’re playing on one chord that you really need to personify and stress to make it interesting.
Well the same with changes, you had to be rhythmical with that too. You have to understand that vertical and horizontal is only as good as the rhythm that you make it be. You know?
You know some things I believe don’t need to be explained.
Yeah, yeah. Buster Williams Junior.
Buster Williams Junior?
Yes. He was the bass player that gave me big trouble in the beginning.
Is he the son of Buster Williams?
No. I mean this is the real Buster Williams.
Oh this is Buster Williams. Wow.
Yeah. Yeah.
Oh. He’s one of my favorites and so he must have been playing, you know like Fender bass instead of —
No, it was an upright bass.
Oh my goodness, wow.
Yeah. Oh I had Ron Carter doing funky lines you know? You look at “Transmogrification” a tune on one of JB’s albums, one of the first albums. And Ron
Carter played the same thing but he played it with so much soul and so much feeling that you thought he was playing “So What.” You know? Yeah.
